Article Title: As Oracle loses $498 billion in less than 10 months, why credit rating agency S&P has identified Sam Altman's OpenAI as a 'key credit risk' for Larry Ellison's company
Article Text:
Why S&P calls OpenAI a 'key credit risk'

Why Oracle's credit rating was downgraded

Here’s what S&P said about OpenAI being a ‘key security risk’ for Oracle

Oracle has lost about $498 billion in market value in less than 10 months. Recently, credit rating agency S&P Global Ratings identified Sam Altman 's OpenAI as a "key credit risk" for the company. In a report explaining its decision to downgrade Oracle's credit rating, S&P said the software giant's aggressive push into AI infrastructure has made it increasingly dependent on a handful of large customers, with OpenAI standing out as the biggest concern. The agency estimates OpenAI accounts for roughly half of Oracle's $638 billion in remaining performance obligations (RPO), warning that if the ChatGPT maker is unable to meet its financial commitments, Oracle could be left with costly data centre leases and weaker cash flow.S&P said Oracle's AI infrastructure business now carries much higher risks than its traditional software business because it requires massive upfront investments in data centres, chips and long-term leases before generating returns.According to the agency, OpenAI represents around 50% of Oracle's $638 billion RPO, making the Microsoft-backed AI company one of Oracle's most important customers. As mentioned anove, S&P warned that OpenAI's ability to honour its contracts depends on continued growth in the AI industry, its ability to raise external funding and whether its AI models remain market leaders."If OpenAI were unable to pay Oracle, we believe Oracle could be left with massive data center leases that it might be unable to exit or have to re-lease to new tenants under less-favorable terms," S&P said.The agency added that it is monitoring OpenAI's financial commitments to data centre operators and chip makers as an indicator of its future financial strength.S&P lowered Oracle's long-term credit rating to 'BBB-' from 'BBB', saying it had underestimated both the scale of Oracle's AI investments and their impact on the company's financial profile.The agency expects Oracle's cloud infrastructure business to grow from 27% of revenue in fiscal 2026 to nearly 60% by fiscal 2028. While that supports future growth, S&P believes it also exposes Oracle to greater financial risk because AI infrastructure requires heavy spending before profits are realised.Oracle has guided capital expenditure of $90 billion to $95 billion for fiscal 2027, far above S&P's earlier estimate of $60 billion.The rating agency now expects Oracle's free operating cash flow deficit to widen to nearly $42 billion in fiscal 2027, compared with its previous forecast of negative $24 billion.OpenAI remains a key credit risk. We estimate that OpenAI makes up roughly half of the $638 billion in RPO. OpenAI’s ability to meet its contractual obligations and raise external financing will be contingent upon AI tailwinds continuing and its models being market leaders. If OpenAI were unable to pay Oracle, we believe Oracle could be left with massive data center leases that it might be unable to exit or have to re-lease to new tenants under less-favorable terms. As a proxy for OpenAI’s future prospects, we’re tracking OpenAI’s financial commitments to data center operators and chip makers to gauge its overall financial exposure and its market share among enterprise and consumers.
Article Summary: S&P Global Ratings downgraded Oracle's long-term credit rating to 'BBB-' from'BBB. S&P said Oracle's aggressive push into AI infrastructure has made it increasingly dependent on a handful of large customers. The agency estimates OpenAI accounts for roughly half of Oracle's $638 billion in remaining performance obligations.

Article Title: As Europe Scientists struggles with heatwave, scientists find alternative to air conditioning, including advances in materials that passively cool buildings
Article Text:
For representative purpose

Why air conditioning cannot be sustainable solution



Solution: Sending heat directly into space



As record-breaking heatwaves sweep across large areas of Europe and Asia, city planners and homeowners are searching for ways to stay cool. While air conditioning remains the go-to fix in nations like the US, Japan, and Australia, scientists warn that installing AC units in every home is an unsustainable trap. Researchers have now highlighted breakthroughs in passive cooling materials, including specialised paints, hydrogel films and radiative coatings, that can lower building temperatures without relying on electricity or overloading power grids.Cooling buildings already accounts for nearly 10% of global electricity consumption, according to a recent review published in Nature Reviews Clean Technology. By 2050, the electricity required to cool indoor spaces is projected to jump by 210%, with greenhouse gas emissions from air conditioning expected to triple.Beyond energy consumption, scientists point out three critical flaws with traditional air conditioning. The first is grid strain that will be caused by massive spikes in AC usage during extreme heatwaves. The second is heat ‘Vicious Loop’. Standard split-system AC units cool indoor rooms by extracting heat and dumping it outdoors.This raises ambient outdoor temperatures in cities, driving higher demand for even more air conditioning.The third is the economic gap. The report says that up to 100 million families across developing regions in India, Mexico, Indonesia, and Brazil will remain unable to afford AC units by 2040, despite having electrical access.“Air conditioning can be life-saving for people at high risk, but the technology has severe drawbacks. We need solutions that don't compound the problem,” explains Matthaios Santamouris, an architecture researcher at the University of New South Wales.Passive cooling technologies require minimal to no power, using advanced material design to regulate building temperatures. The options include automated sun-tracking blinds and window slats that are already common in commercial towers. However, the most promising breakthrough involves passive radiative cooling.This tech takes advantage of the "atmospheric window"—a specific spectrum of heat waves (8 to 13 micrometers) that can pass directly through Earth's atmosphere and escape into space.The first is radiative paints that are infused with microscopic silica and aluminum oxide spheres to scatter solar radiation. This reflects 97% of solar energy and lowers surface temperatures by around 5.26 degrees Celsius.The second solution is evaporative hydrogel films that absorb moisture at night and evaporate water during hot daytime hours while repelling heat. These are claimed to reduce direct sunlight surface temperatures by about 7 degrees Celsius.The researchers say that applying these high-tech coatings to roofs and exterior walls effectively turns whole structures into self-cooling units.“We really need to tackle this problem from different angles,” says urban climatologist Negin Nazarian. By blending advanced materials with smart design, cities can keep residents safe during extreme summer heatwaves without worsening the global climate crisis.
Article Summary: By 2050, the electricity required to cool indoor spaces is projected to jump by 210%, with greenhouse gas emissions from air conditioning expected to triple. Researchers have highlighted breakthroughs in passive cooling materials, including specialised paints, hydrogel films and radiative coatings.

Article Title: Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, Dell, IBM sign joint letter urging US to back open weight AI models: Openness may be one of the most important paths to AI safety
Article Text:
Twenty-five US tech companies want Washington to avoid premature restrictions on open-weight AI models. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google did not sign.

Why 25 American tech companies are defending open-weight AI models right now

Jensen Huang, Satya Nadella and Michael Dell take the argument to social media

OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are the names missing from the list

Twenty-five American technology companies, venture firms and open-source foundations signed a joint letter on Friday asking Washington to leave open-weight AI models alone, arguing that America's lead in artificial intelligence will be settled by how far the technology spreads rather than by who builds the single best model. Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, Dell Technologies, IBM, Palantir, Mistral, Mozilla, the Linux Foundation, Hugging Face, Andreessen Horowitz and Y Combinator are among the names on it.The letter lands in the middle of a fight. The letter arrives while senior Trump administration officials weigh action against Moonshot AI, the Chinese startup whose Kimi K3 model has beaten American systems on several benchmarks this month. The signatories want policymakers to avoid "premature restrictions" that would, in their words, stifle competition or push innovation overseas. Their broader claim is sharper still: openness may be one of the most important paths to AI safety and security, not a threat to it.Open-weight models are the ones anyone can download, inspect, modify and run on their own servers. The letter argues that closed models are not automatically safer, since they can be breached or fail in ways nobody outside the company can see.Concentrating frontier capability behind a handful of providers, the signatories write, creates a small number of single points of failure.The letter also leans on history, drawing a straight line from the open-source software movement of the 1980s to today's argument. Mozilla and the Linux Foundation, two survivors of that era, both signed.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang used his first-ever post on X to share it, writing that open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity while enabling sovereignty. Microsoft's Satya Nadella framed it as a path that protects national security rather than weakening it. Michael Dell said long-term leadership needs choice across the full ecosystem.Elon Musk, whose AI business sits under SpaceX, backed the letter without signing it. "This has my full support," he posted.The three biggest closed-model developers in the US stayed out. Both OpenAI and Anthropic are valued near $1 trillion and have confidentially filed for IPOs that could land this year. Both would benefit if Washington restricted Chinese open models. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman still posted that he was glad to see the letter and wants the US to win in open source and proprietary models alike.The unresolved fight is distillation, the practice of training a smaller model on a stronger one's outputs. White House OSTP director Michael Kratsios accused Moonshot on Wednesday of building Kimi K3 by distilling Anthropic's Fable 5. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went further on Tuesday, comparing it to theft and raising the prospect of sanctions.The letter defends distillation as a normal development technique while conceding that unlawful extraction from closed models is a real problem. Its fix is narrower than a ban. Those cases, it says, belong in targeted legal and commercial frameworks rather than sweeping rules that catch legitimate research in the same net.
Article Summary: Twenty-five US tech companies want Washington to avoid premature restrictions on open-weight AI models. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google did not sign. The letter arrives while senior Trump administration officials weigh action against Moonshot AI, the Chinese startup whose Kimi K3 model has beaten American systems on several benchmarks.

Article Title: Anthropic launches Claude Opus 5, Data shows it is better than Fable 5 that US government restricted
Article Text:
Anthropic Claude Opus 5 benchmarks



Anthropic has launched its newest flagship model, Claude Opus 5, on Friday (July 24), boasting breakthrough performance in coding and knowledge work at half the price of its predecessor. According to company data and industry benchmarks, Opus 5 outperforms Claude Fable 5 – the advanced model previously placed under strict US government export controls – while coming within striking distance of top-tier intelligence at a fraction of the operating cost. This is the company's fourth model launch in less than two months.“Claude Opus 5 provides greatly improved performance for the same cost as its predecessor, Opus 4.8. The charts in this section show how performance changes according to the model’s effort setting, which customers can use to optimize for intelligence or conserve tokens for faster and cheaper results,” the company said.Anthropic positions Opus 5 as a thoughtful, everyday assistant optimised for efficiency. On rigorous coding and knowledge work evaluations, the model establishes new industry standards. According to the data provided by Anthropic through benchmarks, Opus 5 is better than Fable 5 on 10 out of 14 metrics.For example, in software engineering terms on Frontier-Bench, Opus 5 surpasses all competing models, more than doubling the performance of older versions while reducing cost-per-task. On CursorBench 3.2, it performs within 0.5% of Fable 5’s peak score at half the cost.When it comes to problem-solving and automation, on ARC-AGI 3, Opus 5 scored three times higher than the next-best model in solving novel problems. On OSWorld 2.0, Opus 5 outperforms every other tested model, beating Fable 5’s best result at just over one-third of the cost for compute use.“Opus 5 excels on valuable software engineering tasks. For example, on Frontier-Bench v0.1, Opus 5 surpasses all other models, and more than doubles Opus 4.8’s performance at a lower cost per task. On CursorBench 3.2, at max effort, the model performs within 0.5% of Fable 5’s peak score, but at half the cost per task; it also achieves greater performance at a given cost than all other models on high, xhigh, and max effort,” Anthropic added.Despite its coding prowess, Anthropic noted that Opus 5 is intentionally kept behind its sister models on dual-use security evaluations, maintaining safeguards against high-risk cybersecurity threats, as per CNBC.The rollout of Claude Opus 5 arrives as tech companies race to win over enterprise clients who are hesitant to spend heavily on experimental AI without a clear return on investment. Priced at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, the model is designed to provide cost-conscious enterprise clients with high-end capabilities without breaking the budget.With intense pressure mounting from rivals like OpenAI, Google and Amazon even as rapidly advancing open-source Chinese startups, Anthropic's new model serves as the new default option for Claude Max users and the strongest tier available on Claude Pro.
Article Summary: Claude Opus 5 is Anthropic's fourth model launch in less than two months. The model is designed to provide cost-conscious enterprise clients with high-end capabilities without breaking the budget. The rollout comes as tech companies race to win over enterprise clients hesitant to spend heavily on experimental AI without a clear return on investment.

Article Title: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani is hiring software engineers, designers, researchers for his 'tech crew': Here's what the job actually is
Article Text:
NYC mayor wants his ‘tech crew’ to build city software from inside the agency



New York City is betting that in-house tech teams will ship faster and cost less



New York City has opened applications for a new kind of government job. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Monday that the city is recruiting software engineers, product designers, product managers, user researchers, service designers and data experts to staff what he is calling Public Interest Technology Crews—PIT Crews, a pun the mayor committed to by rolling up to the Coney Island go-kart track to make the announcement.The hiring is funded and specific. A City Hall spokesperson confirmed around 30 full-time roles across four crews, supported by $5.24 million in baseline funding in the mayor's new fiscal budget. The listings are live at nyc.gov/pitcrew.A PIT Crew is a mixed team—engineers, designers, product managers, user researchers and data experts—placed alongside staff at a city agency rather than parked in a separate technology department. The crew works with that agency and with New Yorkers to design, build and launch a digital tool, then learn from how people actually use it. The mayor's office describes the timeline as months rather than years, which is the entire premise of the model.Five crews are planned. One handles the Click to Cancel complaint portal, three are attached to Mamdani's affordability and public excellence agenda, and a fifth is being developed with support from The Rockefeller Foundation through the Mayor's Fund to Advance New York City.Zohran Mamdani’s PIT crew’s first assignment is a complaint portal with teethCrew one works with the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection on an online portal where New Yorkers can report companies that make subscriptions near-impossible to cancel. It supports the Click to Cancel rule Mamdani announced last week, which requires businesses to offer the same exit route customers used to sign up. Enforcement begins October 1, and the junk fees ban lands January 1, 2027.The portal is built to do two things at once—give individual New Yorkers a route to recourse, and give City Hall a running database of repeat offenders.Chief Technology Officer and OTI Commissioner Lisa Gelobter framed the roles around a shift in what government technology now is. Every service has a digital surface, she argued, and every confusing step in that surface erodes trust. Her operating instruction for the crews is user first, always, with outcomes weighted over outputs.There is a politics to the hiring as well. NYC-DSA's Tech Action organisers backed the announcement as a choice to build capacity inside government rather than route taxpayer money to consultancies and big tech vendors. BetaNYC's Noel Hidalgo made the cost version of the same argument—in-house teams that deliver faster and cheaper than the outsourced alternative."New Yorkers should not be forced to navigate systems that are confusing, outdated and burdened by bureaucracy," Mamdani said. "The PIT Crew turns that model on its head."Public Interest Technology took shape as a field in the 2010s on a fairly unglamorous premise: government software is usually bad, and fixing it is a staffing and usability problem more than an engineering one. The recruitment page leans into that, pitching the work rather than the salary—the goal, it says, is to make interacting with government dignified and delightful for every New Yorker.
Article Summary: New York City launches Public Interest Technology Crews (PIT Crews) Crews will build city software from inside the agency rather than in a separate department. Hiring is funded by $5.24 million in the mayor's new fiscal budget.

Article Title: One of the popular content creator platforms Patreon lays off 20% employees, CEO says ‘AI not the reason for job cuts’: Read note sent to workers
Article Text:
Patreon lays off 20% employees

Read email that Patreon CEO sent to employees



Hi Team,

I have a painful update this morning. I have decided to reduce the size of our team by 20%, or 93 people. All teammates at the company will receive an email within the next few minutes indicating whether or not your role is impacted by this change.

I’ll get into the reasons for this decision and logistics for the day below, but before I do, I want to acknowledge how painful this will be for the kind, ambitious, hard working, and mission-driven humans who make up this company. The people at Patreon are the core of our spirit and what makes our culture and business so special. Today will be hard for so many people, and as the person responsible for this decision and the decisions leading up to this, I don’t take that lightly. Please take the time you need today to support our departing teammates and yourself.

What’s changing and why

There are two key changes we are making today:

A workforce reduction

Changing our organizational structure and how we work

I’ll explain each below.

1. The workforce reduction

Nothing about our core business has changed – it remains strong and consistent:

More than 300,000 creators in nearly every country in the world are earning money on our platform.

Creators are earning billions of dollars each year on Patreon, and those earnings have continued to exhibit steady, strong growth.

Creators, members, revenue, and processing volume continue to show strong, consistent growth every month.

On top of that, our transformation to becoming a media and community network is starting to work:

Our network is now sending 1.5M new members to creators every month.

Creators have added ~200M free memberships over the past 3 years.

Feed-attributed memberships are up more than 5X since our network launch.

But our transformation is going to take time. We are setting our sights on massive problems: the attention economy is optimizing for addiction instead of long term relationships. Creators are finding it increasingly difficult to reach their followers and build strong communities. The legacy social platforms are locking creators into their systems instead of giving them independence. There is no company better positioned than Patreon to tackle these problems.

At the same time, the market in which we operate has undergone profound change over the last 6 months. We need to adjust our cost structure to ensure that we remain a stable, dependable rock for our creators as we work toward our long term ambition. The changes we're making today are painful, but they're necessary to ensure that Patreon can take the time we need to address the above problems from a position of strength.

2. Changing our organizational structure and how we work

We’re making a number of changes to our organizational structure and how we work. Specifically, we’re flattening the organization, refocusing teams on our top priorities, and evolving key aspects of our operations to make us faster at adapting to change.

We’re making those changes because with a smaller team, we need a new organizational structure to continue executing effectively on our strategy and priorities, which are not changing. We remain focused on:

Improving core creator and fan experiences on the platform, and

Helping creators grow their audiences and businesses through our network

In addition, I want us to have increased agility as a company. AI has fundamentally transformed the tech industry, the pace of change has never been more intense, and I expect it to get even faster. Each of us will play a role in redefining how we work together as the nature of our work continues to change over time.

AI is not a replacement for human creativity

One of the most discussed questions over the last few months has been whether AI is replacing humans.

To be clear about the impact of AI on today’s decision: we are not making the above changes because we believe AI replaces humans.

The more we have learned to use these new tools, the clearer it has become that they are not substitutes for the creativity, judgment, detail orientation, or craftsmanship that our teammates have in spades, nor do they replace the desire for human connection that all of us cherish so deeply. That’s my personal opinion, but more importantly, it’s the foundation of Patreon’s strategy: our product vision and business are both predicated on the value of human creativity and human connection.

AI has fundamentally transformed the tech industry, though, including how we work, how we build products, how we communicate, and more. That does have an impact on how we operate and organize.

Logistics for Today

To our teammates leaving:

In the email you receive from our People team, you’ll find details about next steps, severance packages, and information about how to connect with a member of the People team if you have any questions. You’ll also receive a separate message from a member of our senior leadership team inviting you to a personal call if you would like.

You'll have access to your Patreon laptop and Slack through 5PM PT today. Access to all other internal systems will be removed, because we want to ensure we protect our creators and their businesses.

I know how important it is for folks to be able to say goodbye, so we've created a #gratitude-and-farewell

Slack channel

as a place for all of us to connect, if you feel comfortable.

Severance details:

We’ve prepared a severance package to support impacted employees through this transition:

16 weeks of pay starting from today, including remaining on payroll through our August 20th vesting date.

One additional week of pay for every full year worked at the company.

Additional cash payment to accommodate a) recent hires who haven’t reached their 1-year cliff, and b) more-tenured teammates who haven’t yet received their 2026 refresh grant.

Healthcare

coverage through the end of the year for eligible employees and families.

A $1,500 stipend to replace your company laptop.

Thank you for everything you’ve given our creators, fans, and this company. Your contributions have made a massive difference in the lives of so many people, and I’m deeply grateful for the energy, craft, and care you’ve put into your work. That work is now a part of Patreon and will continue to benefit creators and their communities for years to come.

To our teammates remaining:

The focus for today will be on our departing teammates, but we’ve scheduled a short video call for those of us remaining to be together as a team. Tomorrow, we’ll have an all hands and Q&A to review the details of the reorganization and changes to how we work. Next week, we’ll get together in person as planned to dive deeper on our H2 plans.

For over a decade, Patreon has been growing and evolving to ensure that creators are properly compensated for the value they create in the world. We have successfully adapted and thrived through recessions, the chaos of online media, and multiple market shifts. We continue to come out the other side stronger than before, and that’s exactly what we’ll do again.

Patreon, a popular creator subscription platform, is laying off 20% of its workforce, cutting roughly 93 positions as part of a broader corporate restructuring. The move was first reported by 404 Media and subsequently confirmed in a company-wide memo sent by Patreon CEO Jack Conte. Addressing concerns over the role of automation in the cutbacks, Conte explicitly stated that the job eliminations were not driven by artificial intelligence (AI) replacing human workers, though he acknowledged that AI has fundamentally altered the technological landscape.Conte reassured creators that Patreon’s core business remains “healthy and strong” and that its primary subscription model will not change.He said that the workforce reduction is aimed at streamlining internal management and redirecting resources toward high-priority features. The company is reducing layers of middle management to speed up decision-making, and making changes in key product operations to make the company faster at adapting to market changes.

Article Title: 150-plus Silicon Valley companies have sent a letter to the US government urging not to shut Chinese AI models; warn: Hundreds of American companies will instantly die
Article Text:
Nearly 200 Silicon Valley companies have asked the Trump administration not to cut off US access to Chinese open-weight AI models.

Startup founders say a Chinese AI ban would hand the market to Anthropic and OpenAI

White House escalates rhetoric on Moonshot AI even as blanket ban talk cools

Open-weight AI models expose a growing split between US labs and startups

Nearly 200 Silicon Valley companies, Proton and Y Combinator among them, have written to the Trump administration asking it not to cut off American access to Chinese open-weight AI models. The letters went out Wednesday from the newly formed Little Tech Association, addressed to President Donald Trump, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios. It is the first time the wider startup community has organised itself around this fight, and the timing is not accidental.The trigger was Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion-parameter open-weight model that landed last week and immediately dragged chip stocks down with it. Reports that Washington was weighing a ban on Chinese models followed within days. For founders who build on those models because they cannot afford to spend heavily on credits from Anthropic or OpenAI, the prospect reads less like national security policy and more like an extinction event.Suhail Doshi, founder of AI infrastructure startup Particle and a member of the association, put it without decoration. "There'll be hundreds of companies that instantly die," he told POLITICO."It's great for Anthropic. We're all going to have to spend money on Anthropic."That is the core of the argument. The letter says American leadership needs two things at once: world-leading US open-weight models, and continued access for American builders to open models already circulating globally. Blocking downloads, the founders write, would not slow the spread of Chinese models anywhere else in the world. It would only make US startups poorer and slower.Little Tech Association Executive Director Harry Godfrey wants targeted safeguards rather than blanket prohibitions. "A scalpel rather than a sledgehammer," he said, adding that the question policymakers should be asking is which approach addresses real security concerns without raising costs or limiting access.The administration is not committing either way in public. White House spokesperson Liz Huston said the US leads the world in AI innovation and Trump intends to keep it that way. A White House official, speaking anonymously, was blunter about the leaks: any policy announcement will come directly from the administration, and everything until then is speculation.Senior White House and Cabinet members did discuss the matter Monday night, according to two people familiar with those conversations. But a blanket ban was reportedly never seriously on the table. As of Wednesday, the Commerce Department had not drafted plans to add Chinese AI companies to its Entity List.The rhetoric has kept escalating regardless. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday that the US could sanction Chinese firms found to have improperly distilled American models, citing watermarks from American systems turning up inside Chinese ones. Kratsios went further on Wednesday, alleging Moonshot distilled Anthropic's Fable model while building K3 using a purpose-built internal platform designed to evade detection, and that it acquired Nvidia GB300 servers despite a ban on their sale to Chinese entities. Moonshot has said nothing publicly.Kratsios was careful to say the administration supports open-source frameworks and open-weight models, drawing a line between ordinary distillation and industrial-scale theft. But the fight underneath is about who gets to build.Anthropic has spent months pushing for tighter restrictions on Chinese developers on security grounds. The startups signing this letter say restrictions do nothing to stop proliferation abroad and everything to raise costs at home. Kimi K3's full weights go up on July 27, free to download and modify. Whatever Washington decides after that, it will be deciding late.
Article Summary: Startup founders say a Chinese AI ban would hand the market to Anthropic and OpenAI. The trigger was Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion-parameter open- weight model. Proton and Y Combinator among them, have written to the Trump administration.

Article Title: Andrej Karpathy who coined the term Vibe Coding shares user tips for writing better AI prompts
Article Text:
‘Let AI do the organising’



Read Karpathy’s full post on X (formerly Twitter):



One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos.

..". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

Andrej Karpathy, the prominent artificial intelligence (AI) researcher who famously coined the term “vibe coding,” has a piece of advice for anyone spending hours crafting the “perfect” text prompt for AI: stop trying so hard. Instead of typing out neat, polished instructions, Karpathy suggests users of AI chatbots should simply open the microphone and ramble.In a post on X, the former OpenAI and Tesla executive, who is now a leading AI researcher at Anthropic, revealed that his go-to prompting strategy involves turning on voice mode and talking continuously at a large language model (LLM) for nearly 10 minutes at a time.“Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve,” Karpathy wrote, describing his rambling voice sessions as a “total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness.”According to Karpathy, rambling aloud creates a far better division of labour between human intuition and machine processing power. He said that speaking allows humans to quickly dump every half-formed thought, nuance and goal without getting stuck on phrasing or grammar.The AI takes the chaotic monologue and organises it into clear, actionable and structured outputs. He added that by providing maximum context upfront, users “improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.”
Article Summary: Andrej Karpathy, the AI researcher who coined the term ‘vibe coding,’ suggests users of AI chatbots should simply open the microphone and ramble. He said that speaking allows humans to quickly dump every half-formed thought, nuance and goal without getting stuck on phrasing or grammar.

Article Title: GitHub is tired of 'copy-paste' bug reports; company wants real researchers and here's how much they will get paid now
Article Text:
GitHub halves bug bounty payouts as AI-generated reports flood its security queue

GitHub's new VIP bug bounty program pays $30,000 for critical bugs, but only by invitation

The HackerOne signal requirement gives new researchers just four submissions to prove themselves

Why AI vulnerability scanning is reshaping bug bounty payouts across the industry

GitHub is overhauling the way it pays security researchers, and for most people filing reports, the new numbers sting. From July 27, a critical vulnerability reported through the public bug bounty program will fetch a flat $10,000—down from a range that topped out at $30,000 or more. High-severity findings drop from as much as $20,000 to $5,000. Medium falls to $2,000, and low-severity reports now pay $250, down from a floor of $617.The reason is not subtle. AI tools have made it trivially easy to generate something that looks like a vulnerability report, and GitHub's triage queue has been filling up with exactly that. The Microsoft-owned code host says the restructure is about separating signal from noise. Product security engineer Catherine Cassell framed it as building a program that serious researchers actually find worth their time, and the company's line on the shift is blunt: you don't earn more by submitting more, you earn more by submitting better.Everything GitHub took out of the public program has gone into a permanent private tier. VIP researchers get $1,000 for low findings, $7,500 for medium, $20,000 for high, and $30,000 or more for critical—plus faster responses and direct access to GitHub's security engineering team.Getting in requires a track record. One critical finding qualifies you, or two high, four medium, or seven low. GitHub hasn't said whether there's a time window on that, or whether hitting the threshold guarantees an invitation. Fuller criteria are meant to land on its public HackerOne page.GitHub is also switching on HackerOne's signal requirement for the public program. Researchers who haven't built up a reputation score get a capped number of submissions—four, under HackerOne's standard rules, within a rolling 30-day window.GitHub insists this isn't a wall against newcomers, and that four reports is enough runway for someone with a genuine find. It's a thin margin, though, for anyone still learning GitHub's security model or unlucky enough to have a legitimate bug scored lower than expected.The timing tracks with a wider shift. A day before GitHub's announcement, Google introduced Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber, a model tuned to find and patch vulnerabilities, which it says found 55 confirmed V8 issues in internal testing against 36 for Claude Opus 4.6. Curl maintainer Daniel Stenberg killed his project's cash bounty in January after the confirmed-vulnerability rate fell below 5%.Reports filed before July 27 will be honoured at the old rates, backlog included. Whether the trade-off works is the open question. Cheaper payouts and entry limits should suppress automated junk, but they also concentrate GitHub's closest relationships among researchers already inside the program—narrowing the pool of eyes that made public bounties useful in the first place.
Article Summary: GitHub halts bug bounty payouts as AI-generated reports flood its security queue. From July 27, a critical vulnerability reported through the public bug bounty program will fetch a flat $10,000. VIP researchers get $1,000 for low findings, $7,500 for medium, $20,000 and $30,000 or more for critical.

It’s time for everyone to realize that the fight against data centers has nothing to do with data centers.

They have become a proxy for the hate towards AI and the concentration and accumulation of wealth it’s creating.

Until those running the big LLMs understand this and start a community tour, not to explain the benefits of AI, it’s too late for that, but to help towns and cities that may be impacted by job losses (and I’m a believer their will be a net gains in a few years), this battle is only going to get more intense and let me tell you now , no matter how much money you pay to buy politicians and races, you will lose.

At the same time, I would go to LA and NYC and ask the arts and creative unions what kind of programs would help and protect their artists. DO NOT GO TO THE MUSIC OR FILM COMPANIES. that will make it worse.

Don’t try to pay famous people to endorse what you are doing.

That’s dumb.

Talk to artists and ask them what you can do to provide financial and creative support. Every creative I know is TERRIFIED about what AI will do to their profession. You must meet them face to face and basically do what they say.

The big LLMs have lost the PR battle. Why ? Because they all suck at putting people first. They have an SV attitude that makes them all think they are John Galt saving the

world

Given the number of data centers and power that is needed, today and going forward , If you don’t kiss the asses of the people that go to work every day, and are just trying to pay their bills, you will fall far far short of the capacity you need to make your business work.

American billionaire and former Shark Tank investor Mark Cuban has shared a blunt message for the world’s leading AI companies: start spending billions directly on the people most affected by AI. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Cuban said that firms like Microsoft, Google OpenAI and Anthropic are losing the public relations battle and they need to invest in towns and cities facing job losses due to automation. Across the major LLMs, it’s a cost of doing business,” he wrote. “One thing I have learned is being hated is not good for business.”He also criticised the companies for failing to support workers and creatives, saying that every artist he knows is terrified about AI’s impact on their profession.
